questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
I was actually supposed to go to Russia but due to its war of aggression against Ukraine, that was not an option anymore. KU's international office called me back when the war started, and asked if I was open to other partner universities. Given that I had previously done some writing on the Arctic and was toying with the idea to deepen my knowledge of the region, I told KU I was willing to go to any Arctic country. 
...et voilà, a few months later I found myself attending Vancouver's University of British Columbia.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy. UBC and KU seem to have been long-time partners and both univeristies' international offices were sharing important information timely and easily understandable. Everyone I spoke to was helpful and very kind.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: UBC assigned us international buddies that would show us around campus as well as regularly organize social events.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Overall, orientation assistance was well-organized. However, it was targeted at undergraduate students; being an older Master's student, I had to be more active in collecting relevant information about registering in graduate (aka '5th year' aka 'Master') courses.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: As far I know, only 'Fairview Crescent' and 'Walter Gage' would accept exchange students for on campus housing. I lived in Fairview and it really reminded me of a summer camp with its pretty townhouse-style. When applying for residence, you don't really get to choose your room's size, so rent prices might be higher than expected. Overall, living on campus was cheaper then privately renting a room in the city.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: Apartments came with a kitchen which provided a stove, oven, fridge and microwave.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
The kitchen is empty, so it might come in handy to bring some basic kitchen stuff with you. We bought our kitchen appliances and cuttlery secondhand on facebook marketplace. These additional costs added up quickly, so keep that in mind when planning your stay. 
Also, the rooms are furnished but you'll have to bring your own linens. When offered a room, you will receive additional information on what you need to buy and bring with you.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Living on campus meant that the actual Vancouver area was a 40-minute bus drive away. UBC feels like an isolating island at times, and I would highly recommend leaving the bubble every once in a while. Campus prices are pretty high, and we found ourselves frequently taking the bus to the 'Simon's No Frills' supermarket on Alma Street.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Registration in itself was a bit time-consuming but really manageable. You a have to fill out a form with your top 10 courses you'd like to attend. Don't sweat it though, you can still re-register during the semester's first two weeks.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: When I got to UBC, I attended the undergraduate courses I was originally registered for. They were on Bachelor level, and by emailing the professors of some master seminars, explaining my situation and academic background, I was able to get into very interesting and challenging seminars.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The professors themselves and readings previous reports of exchange students.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: As explained above, it was a bit tedious but very doable.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Talk to professors and the department's secretary directly if you wish to enroll in graduate courses. Be patient, be kind and persistent. If you are planning on doing undergraduate courses, the process is very easy and a no-brainer, thanks to all the resources you'll receive from 'go-global' (UBC's charming name for its international office).

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Loved my graduate classes! The first two weeks that I attended undergraduate classes and thought the teaching style was a bit too theatrical (think dramatic TED-talk). My graduate classes were called 'seminar-style' and indulged in the 'academic boredom aesthetic' that we associate with intellectualism, and miss once it's gone.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: All level of classes require weekly work. The graduate classes were comparable to the level of my master's classes.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: I had to really engage with all the readings and write weekly comments, as well as do a few written assignment, including a bigger one at the end. Participation is also graded, which gives the classes a more lively feel.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
-	Security Challenges for Asian States and People 
-	Development and Institutions 
-	Special Topics in Public Policy: Territorial Disputes and Cross-Border Conflicts

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: "Security Challenges for Asian States and People" was great, as professor Ramana continuesly exposed us to very different readings. Really, any class Ramana teaches, I would highly recommend attending.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
The university transcripts cost 11 dollars. In general, I often felt like a customer rather than a student. There is no subsidized student food on campus (cafeteria style) but rather restaurants and fast food chains, that were often more expensive on than off campus. However, there are plenty of microwaves on campus, so that you can bring your own food. 
Also, housing doesn't really come with appliances, so there were many costs adding up for equipping the kitchen.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Rent, groceries, and renting outdoor equipment.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: You can do everything at UBC, there is social club for any activity you can think of. When doing sports, there are normally two teams: the social clubs and the competitive UBC Thunderbird Teams. The latter does recruiting each season and is not regularly attended by exchange students. The social clubs offer the same sports but without the pressure.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Many self-organized clubs are run by students and only require a small membership fee. I was on the social triathlon team and it was great fun - highly recommend! Free activities include  the swimming pool, and Thunderbird sport events (football, ice hockey and alike).

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Join a club! That way you also get to meet local people and regular students

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Vancouver is super outdoors-y, so there are plenty of hikes in the area. Clubbing is not as big (and quite pricey) but a trip downtown is always nice. Try Earnest ice cream!!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer:
There is plenty of information out there how the academic life is different, and its workload and challenges were not surprising. 'Local culture' was very UBC-focussed; at times it felt like an isolating island since everything was pretty far away from campus. I struggled a bit with the 'exchange student lifestyle'. 
Many of the international exchange students come from wealthy backgrounds and I found myself having to say 'no' more often than I wanted to - plans and trips and hikes were getting a bit excessive and were pricey.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: The social clubs are great for that. And classmates were generally always up for coffee.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The local students are used to a high influx of exchange students. I found it a bit hard to connect, as everyone was very aware we would leave soon.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: There is always something to do and to see. The university and the respective departments always organize plenty of events (go to every 'Open House' of your faculty, the food is normally amazing!).

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Be aware of a) your financial situation b) your academic background and wishes and c) of limiting beliefs you are bringing with you. Just because the academic style is different or things do not seem to make much sense at first, be patient and flexible. Enjoy the otherness!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Sign up for event information of your faculty and join all the facebook groups. Also, don't let FOMO get the best of you

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
My lovely roomies. We became really good friends and shared many emotional moments. 
Also, the seminars were challenging and I found myself cussing the workload at times. However, I learnt so much in a short amount of time and really expanded my academic interests.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The financial challenges and saying no to some plans (FOMO is real).

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Going abroad is always fun! It was easy to tell that UBC and KU have been working together for a while and the administrative process was easily manageable. UBC is a comfortable place to do an exchange semester; I didn't perceive my time as particularly exciting (Raincouver and Vancouver are not too different after all) but it is a good place to go if it is your first itme abroad.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
